newsitem.title: FRANCE: Restructuring started at Nethold - Canal Plus.
newsitem.headline: Restructuring started at Nethold - Canal Plus.

text.p: Restructuring is already underway at Nethold, the Dutch-South African pay television firm which is to merge with French pay TV company Canal Plus on April 1, Canal Plus chairman Pierre Lescure said.

He told an analysts meeting on Canal Plus's 1996 results on Thursday that Nethold management had begun to bring in measures which were provisioned for in Nethold's 1996 accounts and which would therefore not weigh on 1997 figures.
Lescure also said Canal Plus had examined Nethold's accounts "attentively" and there was "nothing dramatic".

"All that reinforces our conviction that we are capable of digesting this merger, of restructuring and redeploying Nethold's activity, and that this (merger) changes not only the dimension of Canal Plus, but also its ability to operate in Europe and its capacity to renew profits," Lescuree said.
Analysts have said that carrying Nethold's losses will undercut Canal Plus's profitablity.
Canal Plus itself on Wednesday predicted that it would only break even in 1997, after posting net attributable profit of 741 million francs for 1996.
However, Nethold will bring an increase of some 20 percent in Canal Plus's 1997 turnover, Canal Plus executives said.

However, executives declined to give any indication of how much integrating Nethold would cost and said analysts should wait until Canal Plus's shareholders meeting scheduled for March 28, when the merger will be discussed.

When Canal Plus announced it agreed to buy Nethold last September, Nethold officials said the company would carry operating losses until end-1998, with break-even expected in 1999. Profits should start to flow from the year 2000.

Analysts questioned by Reuters said Canal Plus including Nethold could nevertheless post profits in 1998, thanks to Canal Plus's strength in France and in the development of digital television, notably in Germany and Spain.
Lescure declined to comment on what he called alarmist comments, made in recent months about the impact of Nethold on Canal Plus's results.
"People have said so many things...it suited them to say that Canal Plus would have difficulties. I refuse to reply to that partially," he said.
"I simply note that the two principal French shareholders, and all Canal Plus board members, have chosen to follow (us). We will reply globally," he said.

French communication group Havas and utilities to communication conglomerate Generale des Eaux were together the main shareholders in Canal Plus, until they agreed to reshuffle their media holdings last month.
Under that deal, Havas becomes the main shareholder in Canal Plus while Generale des Eaux becomes the main shareholder in Havas.
